title: His poems
hookLine: al-Shafi'i also wrote poetry on travel, knowledge and patience

cards: Water that sits still goes bad. Water that runs stays sweet. That line doesn't come from a law book.
It comes from a poem, and tradition puts it in the mouth of the man who wrote the Risalah.

Al-Shafi'i, the jurist who built rules for reading rules, also left verses, or verses gathered under his name: on leaving home, on learning, on waiting out hard days. They're short, plain, and easy to learn by heart.
Today, the jurist as a poet.

teach.h: THE DIWAN: LINES TOLD IN HIS NAME.
teach.b: The collection is called the Diwan of al-Shafi'i. Some readers doubt that every line in it is really his, so, honestly: lines told in his name. Three themes run through them.

teach.h: TRAVEL: THE LION, THE ARROW, THE SUN.
teach.b: First, travel. One poem tells the reader to leave home in search of learning and honor: travel, and you'll find something to replace whatever you left behind. Then the pictures.
Still water spoils; running water stays sweet. A lion that never leaves its den never hunts. An arrow that never leaves the bow never hits.
Even the sun, if it stood still in the sky forever, people would grow tired of it. Second, knowledge. In a short pair of lines, the poet complains to his teacher Waki' about his poor memory.

Waki' tells him to leave sins, because knowledge is a light, and the light of God is not given to one who sins. Study, for him, isn't only hours at a desk; how you live shapes what you can hold. Third, patience.

teach.h: PATIENCE: LET THE DAYS DO AS THEY WILL.
teach.b: Another poem opens by letting the days do whatever they will, and staying calm when the decree comes down. Hard times pass and good times pass; neither one stays.

Together they give a portrait the law books don't: the man who argued line by line about evidence also left home, struggled to remember, and told himself to wait out bad days. Medina with Malik, then Iraq, then Egypt.
He did what the poem says.

how: Verses attributed to al-Shafi'i, gathered in a collection called his Diwan, are read and memorized by students of Islamic learning, especially the lines on travel, memory and patience.

games.q: you're the young student. your memory keeps failing you, so you go to your teacher Waki'. what does he tell you?
o: study longer, late into the night.
leave sins, because knowledge is a light.
give up and learn a trade.
games.why: leave sins, Waki' says: knowledge is a light, and God's light isn't given to one who sins. the cure for memory, in the poem, is a way of living.

practice: Say one line from the travel poem slowly, once: travel, and you'll find something to replace what you leave behind.

Then ask where in your life the water has gone still, a routine, a room, a habit of thought, and what small travel might stir it: a different route home, a new book, a question for someone you don't usually ask.
If you pray, you can ask for a journey that leads somewhere good.

wordCard.voice: His poems. Verses told in al-Shafi'i's name, on travel, on knowledge as a light, and on patience through the days. Today's word.
